# Introduction

`r Biocpkg("ModuleViz")` can be used with an ordered biological axis even when
the axis is not clock time. This vignette demonstrates that workflow on
published CD8 T cell differentiation data.

The other vignette uses the bundled synthetic dataset so it runs offline. This
one is the opposite: it walks through a complete, published, real analysis end
to end, on data anyone can download.

We use two GEO series from the same study of histone modifications in memory
and exhausted CD8 T cells (PubMed
[40389726](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40389726/)):

| Accession | Assay | Samples | What we use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| [GSE285248](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE285248) | RNA-seq | 16 | Defines the temporal modules |
| [GSE285245](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE285245) | CUT&RUN (H3K27ac, H3K27me3) | 86 | Chromatin layer aligned to those modules |

**The experiment.** Naive P14 CD8 T cells were transferred into recipient mice
infected with LCMV Armstrong, which resolves and yields **memory** cells
(harvested day 30), or LCMV Clone 13, which persists and yields **exhausted**
cells (harvested day 32). Spleens were profiled by RNA-seq and by CUT&RUN for
activating (H3K27ac, H3K4me3) and repressive (H3K27me3, H3K9me3) marks.

**The trajectory.** `ModuleViz` was built for time courses, but nothing in it
requires the ordering variable to be wall-clock time. Here the ordered axis is a
*differentiation* axis:

```
TN (naive)  ->  TMEM (memory)  ->  TEX (exhausted)
```

Any ordinal sample axis works the same way: differentiation stages, disease
grades, dose levels, or developmental stages.

> **Chunks in this vignette are not evaluated at build time**, because they
> download data from the NCBI FTP server. Every chunk is runnable as written —
> copy them in order, or run the whole thing at once with
> `Rscript examples/validate_real_data.R` from the package root, which executes
> this exact analysis plus 114 correctness assertions.

# Requirements

```{r requirements}
library(ModuleViz)
library(data.table)
```

Only the small processed count matrices are downloaded, about 4.7 MB in total.
The multi-gigabyte `_RAW.tar` archives on GEO are never touched.

```{r download}
cache_dir <- "geo_cache"
dir.create(cache_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

GEO <- list(
  rna      = list(gse = "GSE285248", file = "GSE285248_NormRC_filter_wanno.txt.gz"),
  h3k27ac  = list(gse = "GSE285245", file = "GSE285245_NormRC_H3K27ac_wID.txt.gz"),
  h3k27me3 = list(gse = "GSE285245", file = "GSE285245_NormRC_H3K27me3_wID.txt.gz")
)

geo_path <- function(entry) {
  dest <- file.path(cache_dir, entry$file)
  if (!file.exists(dest)) {
    url <- sprintf("https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/series/%snnn/%s/suppl/%s",
                   substr(entry$gse, 1, 6), entry$gse, entry$file)
    utils::download.file(url, dest, mode = "wb")
  }
  dest
}

paths <- lapply(GEO, geo_path)
```

# Read The RNA-seq Matrix

The RNA table carries six annotation columns (`Chr`, `Start`, `End`, `Geneid`,
`Gene.Name`, `Strand`) followed by the 16 sample columns. A handful of gene
symbols appear under more than one Ensembl ID, so we keep the most highly
expressed copy of each symbol and use symbols as rownames.

```{r read-rna}
rna_raw  <- fread(paths$rna)
rna_cols <- grep("_RNA_", names(rna_raw), value = TRUE)

rna_raw[, .mean_expr := rowMeans(as.matrix(.SD)), .SDcols = rna_cols]
setorder(rna_raw, Gene.Name, -.mean_expr)
rna_uniq <- rna_raw[!duplicated(Gene.Name)]

rna_mat <- as.matrix(rna_uniq[, ..rna_cols])
rownames(rna_mat) <- rna_uniq$Gene.Name

dim(rna_mat)
```

```
#> [1] 16429    16
```

# Build The Sample Metadata

`ModuleViz` needs one row per sample with a sample ID and a **numeric** ordering
column. The GEO column names encode everything we need in the pattern
`<Infection>_P14_Day<d>_<assay>_Rep<n>_S<n>`, so the metadata can be parsed
straight out of them. Writing this as a function pays off later, because the
CUT&RUN tables follow exactly the same naming scheme.

```{r metadata}
make_meta <- function(cols, assay) {
  infection <- sub("_P14_.*", "", cols)
  day       <- as.integer(sub(".*_Day([0-9]+)_.*", "\\1", cols))
  state     <- c(Naive = "TN", Arm = "TMEM", Cl13 = "TEX")[infection]
  data.table(
    SampleID   = cols,
    State      = factor(state, levels = c("TN", "TMEM", "TEX")),
    # the ordered differentiation axis handed to time_col
    StateOrder = unname(c(TN = 1, TMEM = 2, TEX = 3)[state]),
    # naive cells are the pre-infection baseline, so they sit at day 0
    Day        = ifelse(infection == "Naive", 0L, day),
    Replicate  = as.integer(sub(".*_Rep([0-9]+)_.*", "\\1", cols)),
    Assay      = assay
  )
}

rna_meta <- make_meta(rna_cols, "RNA")
rna_meta[, .N, by = .(State, Day)]
```

```
#>     State   Day     N
#>    <fctr> <int> <int>
#> 1:     TN     0     8
#> 2:   TMEM    30     4
#> 3:    TEX    32     4
```

`StateOrder` is the key column: it is what `time_col` will point at, and it is
what makes the modules come out ordered naive-high through exhaustion-high.

Note that there are **eight** naive samples, not four. Naive cells were profiled
twice, once alongside each infection, so they serve as the day-matched baseline
for both arms. That imbalance is fine — nothing in `ModuleViz` requires equal
group sizes.

# Select Differentially Expressed Genes

Real analyses do not cluster the whole transcriptome. Clustering 16,429 genes
would bury the interesting structure under thousands of flat, uninformative
profiles. We select the genes that actually move across the three states.

A vectorised one-way ANOVA across `TN` / `TMEM` / `TEX` is fast and needs no
extra packages. If you already have `DESeq2` or `edgeR` results for this
comparison, substitute them here — all that matters downstream is a set of gene
IDs and, optionally, a ranking statistic.

```{r deg}
log_rna <- log2(rna_mat + 1)

deg_anova <- function(x, grp) {
  grp <- factor(grp)
  n <- ncol(x); k <- nlevels(grp)
  grand <- rowMeans(x)
  ssb <- 0; ssw <- 0
  for (g in levels(grp)) {
    cols <- which(grp == g)
    mg   <- rowMeans(x[, cols, drop = FALSE])
    ssb  <- ssb + length(cols) * (mg - grand)^2
    ssw  <- ssw + rowSums((x[, cols, drop = FALSE] - mg)^2)
  }
  df1 <- k - 1; df2 <- n - k
  Fstat <- (ssb / df1) / (ssw / df2)
  Fstat[!is.finite(Fstat)] <- 0
  data.table(
    ID     = rownames(x),
    Fstat  = Fstat,
    pvalue = stats::pf(Fstat, df1, df2, lower.tail = FALSE),
    padj   = stats::p.adjust(stats::pf(Fstat, df1, df2, lower.tail = FALSE),
                             method = "BH")
  )
}

state_of <- rna_meta$State[match(colnames(log_rna), rna_meta$SampleID)]
deg <- deg_anova(log_rna, state_of)

mean_by <- function(s) rowMeans(log_rna[, state_of == s, drop = FALSE])
deg[, `:=`(
  log2FC_TMEM_vs_TN  = mean_by("TMEM") - mean_by("TN"),
  log2FC_TEX_vs_TN   = mean_by("TEX")  - mean_by("TN"),
  log2FC_TEX_vs_TMEM = mean_by("TEX")  - mean_by("TMEM"),
  baseMean           = rowMeans(rna_mat)
)]
deg[, maxAbsLFC := pmax(abs(log2FC_TMEM_vs_TN), abs(log2FC_TEX_vs_TN),
                        abs(log2FC_TEX_vs_TMEM))]

sig <- deg[padj < 0.01 & maxAbsLFC >= 1 & baseMean >= 10]
setorder(sig, -Fstat)
nrow(sig)
```

```
#> [1] 4176
```

4,176 genes pass. We keep the top 3,000 by ANOVA *F* so the vignette runs
quickly; raise or drop the cap freely.

```{r deg-matrix}
sig <- sig[seq_len(min(3000, nrow(sig)))]

# Cluster on the log scale: z-scoring raw counts lets a few high-count
# outliers dominate the distance metric.
deg_mat <- log2(rna_mat[sig$ID, , drop = FALSE] + 1)

head(sig$ID, 12)
```

```
#>  [1] "Pik3ap1" "Myo1f"   "Chsy1"   "Gnptab"  "Ccr9"    "Satb1"
#>  [7] "Rapgef6" "Il6ra"   "Sytl2"   "Ccr5"    "Tox"     "Fam169b"
```

`Tox`, the master transcription factor of CD8 T cell exhaustion, is already in
the top 12 — a good sign that the selection is picking up real biology.

# Choose The Number Of Modules

```{r choose-k}
z <- zscore_rows(deg_mat)

K <- 6   # see the note below
diag <- choose_k(z, k_range = 2:12, method = "kmeans",
                 file = "choose_k_elbow.pdf")
diag
attr(diag, "suggested_k")
```

```
#>         k tot_withinss mean_silhouette elbow_k
#>  1:     2    10243.402       0.6761535       5
#>  2:     3     7723.609       0.5215970       5
#>  3:     4     6094.619       0.3693580       5
#>  4:     5     5088.006       0.3522561       5
#>  5:     6     4378.953       0.3252019       5
#>  ...
#> [1] 5
```

The elbow lands at k = 5, but we use **k = 6**. This is worth being explicit
about, because it is the most common judgement call in this workflow.

At k = 5 there is **no memory-peaking module at all**: the TMEM-specific
programme is absorbed into its neighbours, so the modules run naive -> naive ->
naive -> exhausted -> exhausted. Since memory-versus-exhaustion is the
comparison this study exists to make, k = 5 would hide the result. At k = 6 a
module with a clear TMEM peak appears (Cluster4 below), and every module still
has a stability above 0.9.

The elbow is a heuristic; a k that merges two biologically distinct programmes
is worse than one that splits a module in two. If you want the figure itself to
record the k you settled on, `choose_k(..., chosen_k = K)` draws it as a solid
line beside the dashed elbow, and `annotate_k = FALSE` strips both markers for a
bare curve.

# Cluster Into Temporal Modules

```{r cluster}
obj <- longitudinal_cluster(
  deg_mat, rna_meta,
  sample_col = "SampleID",
  time_col   = "StateOrder",   # the ordered differentiation axis
  k          = K,
  method     = "kmeans",
  stability  = TRUE,
  n_resample = 20,
  seed       = 1
)

obj
obj$stability
```

```
#> <longi>  3000 features x 16 samples,  6 modules (kmeans)
#>   stability (mean Jaccard): 0.90 - 0.97
#>     Cluster MeanJaccard     N
#> 1: Cluster1       0.958   388
#> 2: Cluster2       0.975   776
#> 3: Cluster3       0.972   158
#> 4: Cluster4       0.901   243
#> 5: Cluster5       0.958  1019
#> 6: Cluster6       0.968   416
```

Every module has a mean Jaccard above 0.9 under resampling, so all six are
reproducible. Values below roughly 0.6 would mean a module is an artefact of one
particular clustering run and should not be interpreted.

Modules are automatically renumbered so that `Cluster1` peaks earliest and
`Cluster6` peaks latest:

```{r centroids}
cent <- as.matrix(obj$centroids[, -1])
rownames(cent) <- obj$centroids$Cluster
colnames(cent) <- c("TN", "TMEM", "TEX")
round(cent, 2)
```

```
#>            TN  TMEM   TEX
#> Cluster1  0.74 -0.01 -1.48   <- naive-high, lost on activation
#> Cluster2  0.92 -0.87 -0.98   <- naive-specific
#> Cluster3  0.53 -1.53  0.46   <- down in memory, partly restored in exhaustion
#> Cluster4 -0.83  1.31  0.34   <- memory-specific
#> Cluster5 -0.92  0.69  1.15   <- shared effector, highest in exhaustion
#> Cluster6 -0.65 -0.26  1.55   <- exhaustion-specific
```

# Check The Modules Against Known Biology

This is the step worth doing before any figure goes into a paper. Canonical
markers should land where the biology says they should.

```{r biology}
module_of <- setNames(as.character(obj$cluster), rownames(obj$z))

TEX_MARKERS <- c("Pdcd1", "Tox", "Havcr2", "Lag3", "Entpd1", "Cd101", "Cd160")
TN_MARKERS  <- c("Sell", "Ccr7", "Lef1", "Tcf7")

data.table(Gene = TEX_MARKERS, Module = module_of[TEX_MARKERS])
data.table(Gene = TN_MARKERS,  Module = module_of[TN_MARKERS])
```

```
#>      Gene   Module          #>      Gene   Module
#> 1:  Pdcd1 Cluster6          #> 1:   Sell Cluster2
#> 2:    Tox Cluster6          #> 2:   Ccr7 Cluster2
#> 3: Havcr2 Cluster5          #> 3:   Lef1 Cluster1
#> 4:   Lag3 Cluster6          #> 4:   Tcf7 Cluster1
#> 5: Entpd1 Cluster5
#> 6:  Cd101 Cluster6
#> 7:  Cd160 Cluster5
```

Every inhibitory-receptor and exhaustion gene falls in Cluster5 or Cluster6, the
two exhaustion-peaking modules. Every naive/stemness gene falls in Cluster1 or
Cluster2, the naive-peaking modules. The clustering recovered the expected
programme without being told anything about it.

# Draw The Heatmap

Three palettes are in play, and each is chosen for its job:

- `cluster_palette` — a **qualitative** palette for module identity (`"paired"`,
  `"set2"`, `"set3"`, `"okabe_ito"`, ...).
- `annotation_palette` — a qualitative palette for categorical metadata bars.
  `"set2"` is the default; use `"set3"` beyond eight levels.
- `zscore_palette` — a **continuous** scale for the matrix body: `"viridis"`
  (perceptually uniform and colour-blind safe) or `"rdbu"` (diverging). This
  walkthrough uses one scheme throughout; change the single argument to swap it.

```{r heatmap}
rank_tab <- sig[, .(ID, value = -log10(pmax(padj, .Machine$double.xmin)))]

longitudinal_heatmap(
  obj,
  annotation_cols    = c("State", "Day"),
  rank_table         = rank_tab,   # label the most significant genes per module
  id_field           = "ID",
  value_field        = "value",
  top_n_label        = 3,
  zscore_palette     = "viridis",  # <- "rdbu" for the diverging alternative
  cluster_palette    = "paired",
  annotation_palette = "set2",
  # the GEO sample IDs are long and the State bar already says what each
  # column is, so suppress them and scale the remaining text up for print
  show_column_names        = FALSE,
  label_fontsize           = 13,
  row_title_fontsize       = 13,
  annotation_name_fontsize = 13,
  legend_fontsize          = 12,
  title_fontsize           = 16,
  title  = "CD8 T cell differentiation: DEG modules (GSE285248)",
  file   = "cd8_module_heatmap.png",
  width  = 10,
  height = 12
)
```

![CD8 T cell DEG modules](figures/cd8_01_module_heatmap.png)

Rows are split by module and ordered early-peaking to late-peaking; columns run
naive, memory, exhausted. The `Stability` bar on the left encodes each module's
Jaccard score, and row titles carry both module size and stability.

Note the two ways of choosing labels. `rank_table` + `top_n_label` labels the
top *n* genes per module by a statistic you supply, which is usually what you
want for a figure; `label_features` labels an explicit list of genes. The two
can be combined.

# Plot Module Trajectories

```{r lineplot}
pattern_lineplot(
  obj, cluster_palette = "paired", base_size = 15,
  title_fontsize = 14,
  # the ordering column is an integer rank, so relabel the axis with the
  # state names it stands for
  xlab        = "Differentiation state",
  time_labels = c("1" = "TN", "2" = "TMEM", "3" = "TEX"),
  x_angle     = 0,
  file = "cd8_module_patterns.pdf"
)
```

![Mean z-score trajectory per module](figures/cd8_03_module_patterns.png)

# Check Module Coherence

Clustering guarantees that a module's genes are closer to each other than to
other modules. It does not guarantee they actually agree. Correlating every
gene in a module against every other one shows whether the module is one
programme or several averaging together.

```{r coherence}
module_correlation_summary(obj)
```

```
#>     Cluster     N NShown MeanCor
#> 1: Cluster1   388    388   0.876
#> 2: Cluster2   776    776   0.916
#> 3: Cluster3   158    158   0.829
#> 4: Cluster4   243    243   0.857
#> 5: Cluster5  1019   1019   0.931
#> 6: Cluster6   416    416   0.886
```

Every module sits between 0.83 and 0.93, so all six are internally coherent. A value below
roughly 0.3, or visible sub-blocks in the heatmap below, would mean the module
should be split by raising `k`.

```{r coherence-heatmap}
module_correlation_heatmap(
  obj,
  clusters        = "Cluster6",   # the exhaustion-specific module
  # every gene in the module is used by default; printing 416 row names would
  # be unreadable, so only the 30 strongest-signal genes get labelled
  label_top_n     = 30,
  corr_palette    = "rdbu",   # correlations diverge around 0
  label_fontsize  = 9,
  legend_fontsize = 12,
  title_fontsize  = 11,
  file = "cd8_correlation.png", width = 7.5, height = 7
)
```

![Gene-gene correlation inside the exhaustion module](figures/cd8_05_module_correlation.png)

A `.pdf` destination writes one page per module instead:

```{r coherence-pdf}
module_correlation_heatmap(obj, file = "cd8_module_correlations.pdf")
```

# Export The Tables

```{r export}
write_memberships(obj, prefix = "cd8_modules")
```

Writes `cd8_modules_memberships.txt` (gene to module), `_centroids.txt` (mean
trajectory per module), and `_stability.txt`. The membership table is what you
would feed into GO or GSEA enrichment, one module at a time.

# Add The CUT&RUN Layer

Now the paired-omics question: does chromatin state track these expression
modules?

The CUT&RUN tables give peak coordinates but **no gene symbol**, so peaks have
to be assigned to genes first. We map each peak to its nearest gene
transcription start site, using the coordinates already present in the RNA
annotation, and keep peaks within 25 kb.

```{r peak-mapping}
gene_tss <- unique(rna_uniq[, .(Chr,
                                TSS  = ifelse(Strand == "+", Start, End),
                                Gene = Gene.Name)])

map_peaks_to_nearest_gene <- function(peaks, genes, max_dist = 25000) {
  out <- list()
  for (ch in intersect(unique(peaks$Chr), unique(genes$Chr))) {
    gg <- genes[Chr == ch][order(TSS)]
    pp <- peaks[Chr == ch]
    if (!nrow(gg) || !nrow(pp)) next
    i  <- findInterval(pp$Mid, gg$TSS)
    lo <- pmax(i, 1L); hi <- pmin(i + 1L, nrow(gg))
    dlo <- abs(pp$Mid - gg$TSS[lo]); dhi <- abs(pp$Mid - gg$TSS[hi])
    pick <- ifelse(dlo <= dhi, lo, hi)
    out[[length(out) + 1L]] <- data.table(peakN = pp$peakN,
                                          Gene  = gg$Gene[pick],
                                          dist  = pmin(dlo, dhi))
  }
  rbindlist(out)[dist <= max_dist]
}
```

`dual_omics_heatmap()` recovers the gene from a secondary row ID using
`gene_of_secondary`, whose default is `sub("^.*_", "", id)` — everything after
the last underscore. So we name the rows `peak1243_Pdcd1` and the default just
works.

```{r load-cutrun}
load_cutrun <- function(path, mark) {
  tab   <- fread(path)
  scols <- grep(paste0("_", mark, "_Rep"), names(tab), value = TRUE)
  pk    <- tab[, .(peakN, Chr, Mid = as.integer((Start + End) / 2))]
  ann   <- map_peaks_to_nearest_gene(pk, gene_tss)
  tab   <- tab[peakN %in% ann$peakN]
  ann   <- ann[match(tab$peakN, peakN)]
  m     <- as.matrix(tab[, ..scols])
  rownames(m) <- paste0(ann$peakN, "_", ann$Gene)   # PeakID_SYMBOL
  list(mat = log2(m + 1), meta = make_meta(scols, mark), ann = ann)
}

ac <- load_cutrun(paths$h3k27ac, "H3K27ac")
dim(ac$mat)
```

```
#> [1] 20879    16
```

A gene can carry several peaks; `aggregate = "mean"` averages a gene's peaks,
`aggregate = "top"` takes the single strongest one.

```{r dual-omics}
ac_obj <- longitudinal_cluster(ac$mat, ac$meta,
                               sample_col = "SampleID",
                               time_col   = "StateOrder",
                               k = 4, stability = FALSE)

d_ac <- dual_omics_heatmap(
  primary        = obj,        # RNA drives the module structure and row order
  secondary      = ac_obj,     # chromatin is shown in that same order
  primary_name   = "RNA",
  secondary_name = "H3K27ac",
  aggregate      = "mean",
  label_features = c(TEX_MARKERS, TN_MARKERS),
  zscore_palette  = "viridis",
  cluster_palette = "paired",
  show_column_names  = FALSE,
  label_fontsize     = 13,
  row_title_fontsize = 13,
  legend_fontsize    = 12,
  title_fontsize     = 16,
  file = "cd8_rna_vs_h3k27ac.png", width = 15, height = 12
)
```

![RNA modules with matched H3K27ac signal](figures/cd8_04_rna_vs_h3k27ac.png)

The chromatin panel mirrors the expression panel block for block. The
naive-high modules carry naive-high H3K27ac; the exhaustion-high module
containing *Pdcd1*, *Tox*, and *Lag3* carries exhaustion-high H3K27ac. The
activating mark is deposited where the genes are expressed.

The repressive mark behaves differently, which is the point of the comparison:

```{r repressive}
me3 <- load_cutrun(paths$h3k27me3, "H3K27me3")

d_me3 <- dual_omics_heatmap(
  primary = obj, secondary = me3$mat,     # a raw matrix also works
  primary_name = "RNA", secondary_name = "H3K27me3",
  label_features = TEX_MARKERS,
  file = "cd8_rna_vs_h3k27me3.png", width = 15, height = 12
)
```

Quantifying the contrast over the exhaustion-induced genes:

```{r concordance}
peak_state <- setNames(colnames(cent)[apply(cent, 1, which.max)], rownames(cent))
tex_genes  <- names(module_of)[peak_state[module_of] == "TEX"]

delta_in <- function(res, meta_tab, genes) {
  zs   <- res$z_secondary
  keep <- intersect(genes, rownames(zs))
  st   <- meta_tab$State[match(colnames(zs), meta_tab$SampleID)]
  mean(zs[keep, st == "TEX"], na.rm = TRUE) -
    mean(zs[keep, st == "TN"],  na.rm = TRUE)
}

round(c(H3K27ac  = delta_in(d_ac,  ac$meta,  tex_genes),
        H3K27me3 = delta_in(d_me3, me3$meta, tex_genes)), 3)
```

```
#>  H3K27ac H3K27me3
#>    1.350   -0.032
```

The activating mark is gained at exhaustion-induced genes; the repressive mark
is flat to slightly lost. Chromatin accessibility tracks the expression
modules, which is exactly the claim the original study makes.

# Reproducing Everything

The complete script, with 114 assertions covering data integrity, clustering
correctness, palette behaviour, marker-gene placement, and cross-omics
concordance, ships with the package:

```{r reproduce, eval=FALSE}
# from the package root
system("Rscript examples/validate_real_data.R")
```

It caches the downloads under `examples/outputs/geo_cache/`, so re-runs are
offline and fast.

# Adapting This To Your Own Data

The only project-specific parts are steps 2 to 4. Everything from step 5 onward
is generic. To reuse the workflow you need:

1. A numeric feature-by-sample matrix with feature IDs as rownames.
2. A metadata table with a sample ID column matching the matrix columns, and a
   **numeric** ordering column for `time_col` (real time, or an ordinal stage
   as here).
3. Optionally, a `group_col` for a second factor such as genotype or treatment
   arm, which splits the heatmap columns and facets the line plot.
4. Optionally, a secondary matrix whose rownames end in `_<GeneSymbol>`, or a
   custom `gene_of_secondary` function.
